title: How Close is ChatGPT to Human Experts? Comparison Corpus, Evaluation, and Detection
extended_summary:
This paper asks how close ChatGPT is to human experts in question-answering quality, what linguistic differences distinguish its outputs from human-written answers, and how well automated systems can detect ChatGPT-generated text. The authors frame these questions around the rapid spread of generative AI and the risks of AI-generated content on online platforms, including concerns about accuracy, reliability, and misuse.

The core contribution is the Human ChatGPT Comparison Corpus (HC3), a large bilingual dataset of question-answer pairs collected from existing QA sources and Wikipedia-style materials, with both human answers and ChatGPT answers for the same prompts. The paper then reports human evaluations (Turing-style detection and helpfulness judgments) and linguistic analyses comparing the two sources across domains such as open-domain QA, computer science, medicine, finance, psychology, and law.

The study is not an educational intervention study; it does not involve schools, teachers, or students. Instead, it evaluates content quality and detectability in a general QA setting. The main findings are that ChatGPT is often more organized, longer, and more neutral than humans, but can still fabricate facts in domain-specific contexts. The authors also show that RoBERTa-based detectors generally outperform simpler GLTR-style methods, that sentence-level detection is harder than full-text detection, and that adding question context improves detection robustness.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational LLM chatbot based on the GPT-3.5 series, fine-tuned with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) to generate responses to user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the focal generative model for comparison against human expert answers in the HC3 corpus, and as the source of text to evaluate detectability and linguistic characteristics.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports human evaluation results comparing ChatGPT answers with human answers across multiple QA domains. Expert Turing-test detection rates for ChatGPT-generated answers were 0.90 overall for paired text and 0.81 overall for single-text English, while amateurs reached 0.48 overall on single-text English; helpfulness tests found ChatGPT was judged more helpful than human answers in 0.57 overall of English cases and 0.54 overall of Chinese cases. The paper also reports that ChatGPT can be easier to detect when a human answer pair is shown, and that it is generally more helpful than humans in finance and psychology but less helpful in medicine.
findings.measure: Human evaluation: Turing test detection accuracy and helpfulness preference in domain-specific QA

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-study empirical comparison with human evaluation and linguistic analysis, not a controlled educational intervention study. The methods are systematic but the outcome is not an education outcome and no causal effect on learning is tested.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported results show detectable differences and modest helpfulness preferences, but there is no educational effect size tied to instruction or learning. The paper is mainly about text characteristics and detection performance rather than instructional impact.
